problem: The sign given for heat leaked to the room is wrong. The steady balance gives S_gen = (entropy out with streams) − (entropy in with streams) − Σ Q_j/T_j. A room loss has Q_room negative, so the term actually added to S_gen is −Q_room/T_room, a positive number. Telling students to 'add Q_room/T_room with Q_room negative if it leaves' makes them subtract entropy and under-count S_gen, which can even hide a second-law violation.
fix: If the exchanger also loses heat to the room, the leak raises the generation: S_gen = m_h(s_h,out − s_h,in) + m_c(s_c,out − s_c,in) − Q_room/T_room, with Q_room negative when heat leaves, so the last term is positive.

problem: The formula Σ Q_j/T_j assumes each boundary j is at one uniform absolute temperature. Real boundaries (a boiler wall, a duct surface) often vary in temperature, and dividing total Q by one T gives the wrong entropy flow.
fix: Add one line: T_j is the uniform absolute temperature of boundary j in K; if the boundary temperature varies, replace Q_j/T_j by the integral ∫ δQ/T over that boundary.

problem: The state is named precisely (2 MPa, 400 °C) but the entropy quoted, 7.0 kJ/(kg·K), is not the steam-table value for that state (about 7.13 kJ/(kg·K)). A student who checks tables will think the data are wrong.
fix: Say the entropy values are chosen for easy arithmetic, e.g. 'Take s_in = 7.0 kJ/(kg·K) and s_out = 7.4 kJ/(kg·K) as the given data (rounded for arithmetic)', so no one expects them to match the tables at 2 MPa, 400 °C.

problem: Pinch analysis for heat-exchanger networks is mainly an energy-targeting method (composite curves, minimum utility). Saying it 'uses the same flow-entropy bookkeeping' overstates the link; only exergy-based variants bring entropy in.
fix: Write: exergy-based variants of heat-exchanger network pinch analysis also track entropy generation stream by stream to reduce utility use.
